body:
Formation of the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association

The Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA) emerged in September 1928 when revolutionary nationalists reorganised the earlier Hindustan Republican Association.

An important meeting took place at Feroz Shah Kotla in Delhi. The organisation adopted socialism as an explicit political objective.

The name is generally expanded as Hindustan Socialist Republican Association, although some contemporary and textbook accounts also use Hindustan Socialist Republican Army for the revolutionary organisation.

The HSRA opposed British colonial domination and sought a republic in which workers and peasants would not be subjected to economic exploitation. Its members increasingly argued that genuine political change required public awareness and broader participation rather than isolated revolutionary actions alone.

Principal Leaders and Associates

  • Chandrashekhar Azad: A leading organiser and revolutionary commander associated with the reconstituted movement.
  • Bhagat Singh: A major political thinker and organiser who connected the demand for independence with socialist ideas.
  • Sukhdev Thapar: An important revolutionary organiser associated with Punjab and the HSRA.
  • Shivaram Hari Rajguru: A revolutionary associated with the killing of British police officer J. P. Saunders.
  • Batukeshwar Dutt: Bhagat Singh's associate in the Central Legislative Assembly bombing of 1929.
  • Bhagwati Charan Vohra: Another important member of the revolutionary organisation.

Bhagat Singh's Political Activities

Bhagat Singh was born in 1907 in Punjab. He belonged to a family connected with the nationalist movement and became interested in revolutionary politics at an early age.

He helped establish the Naujawan Bharat Sabha in Lahore in 1926. It aimed to mobilise young people and spread nationalist political awareness. This organisation should be distinguished from the HSRA, which was reorganised in 1928.

Bhagat Singh studied political movements and socialist ideas. He increasingly argued that revolution meant changing an exploitative political and social system, not merely replacing individual British officials or carrying out acts of violence.

The Saunders Killing: 17 December 1928

Background: The Simon Commission Protest

The British government appointed the Simon Commission in 1927 to examine constitutional reforms in India. The commission had no Indian members, which generated widespread opposition.

During a protest against the commission in Lahore on 30 October 1928, police used a lathi charge against demonstrators led by Lala Lajpat Rai. He suffered injuries and died on 17 November 1928.

Revolutionary Retaliation

Bhagat Singh and his associates sought to retaliate against the police action. On 17 December 1928, the British police officer J. P. Saunders was killed in Lahore.

Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Chandrashekhar Azad were associated with this action.

The revolutionaries had intended to target James A. Scott, the police officer they regarded as responsible for the lathi charge. Saunders was killed instead.

Lala Lajpat Rai: Nationalist leader injured during the anti-Simon Commission protest and died in November 1928.
J. P. Saunders: British police officer killed in Lahore on 17 December 1928.
James A. Scott: Police officer whom the revolutionaries had originally intended to target.

Central Legislative Assembly Bombing: 8 April 1929

On 8 April 1929, Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt threw bombs in the Central Legislative Assembly in Delhi.

The action was intended as a political demonstration rather than an attempt to cause mass casualties. The revolutionaries opposed measures including the Public Safety Bill and the Trade Disputes Bill, which they regarded as threats to political freedoms and workers' rights.

They distributed political leaflets and deliberately remained available for arrest. Their intention was to use the subsequent trial to publicise their political ideas.

The leaflet expressed the purpose of the demonstration through the phrase make the deaf hear.

This incident must be distinguished from the killing of Saunders. The Saunders action occurred in Lahore in 1928, whereas the Assembly bombing occurred in Delhi in 1929.

Trials, Imprisonment and Executions

Assembly Bomb Case and Lahore Conspiracy Case

Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt faced prosecution for the Assembly bombing. Investigations into the Saunders killing also resulted in the Lahore Conspiracy Case, which involved Bhagat Singh and several other revolutionaries.

The accused used the court proceedings to express their opposition to British rule. Revolutionary prisoners also protested against prison conditions and demanded treatment as political prisoners.

Jatindra Nath Das, also known as Jatin Das, died in prison on 13 September 1929 following a prolonged hunger strike.

Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were sentenced to death in the Lahore Conspiracy Case. All 3 were executed at Lahore Jail on 23 March 1931.

Batukeshwar Dutt, who had participated in the Assembly bombing, was not one of the 3 revolutionaries executed on that date.

Chandrashekhar Azad's Final Encounter

Chandrashekhar Azad had participated in the Kakori action and played an important leadership role in the HRA's later reorganisation.

On 27 February 1931, Azad died during an encounter with British police at Alfred Park in Allahabad, now Prayagraj. The park is now known as Chandrashekhar Azad Park.

Azad's death occurred before the execution of Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru on 23 March 1931.

Prelims focus

  • HSRA: September 1928, Feroz Shah Kotla, Delhi.
  • Bhagat Singh helped establish the Naujawan Bharat Sabha in Lahore in 1926.
  • J. P. Saunders was killed in Lahore on 17 December 1928.
  • Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt carried out the Central Legislative Assembly bombing on 8 April 1929.
  • Chandrashekhar Azad died at Alfred Park on 27 February 1931.
  • Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were executed on 23 March 1931.
  • Trap: Saunders was killed instead of the intended target, James A. Scott. Batukeshwar Dutt was not among the 3 executed on 23 March 1931.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-III, Class 8, chapter The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed p. 120; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World-II, Class 10, chapter Nationalism in India, printed p. 65; Indira Gandhi National Open University, History of India VIII (c. 1857–1950), Unit 9, sections 9.7–9.8, printed pp. 125–128, consulted 21 November 2026; Government of Tamil Nadu, SCERT, Higher Secondary Second Year History, Vol. 1, 2019, Unit 5, printed pp. 66–67; Allahabad Museum, Government of India, Museums of India repository, Chandrashekhar Azad historical encounter record, consulted 21 November 2026.]

title: HSRA, Bhagat Singh and Chandrashekhar Azad: Revolutionary Activity from 1928 to 1931

body:
Chittagong and the Revolutionary Movement

Chittagong was an important port town in eastern Bengal under British colonial rule. It is now part of Bangladesh.

Revolutionary activity in Bengal continued after the decline of some earlier organisations. A younger generation increasingly considered coordinated revolutionary action as an alternative to isolated attacks against individual colonial officers.

The most important leader of this development in Chittagong was Surya Sen, popularly known as Masterda.

Surya Sen and His Organisation

Surya Sen was a schoolteacher who became an important revolutionary organiser in Chittagong. He had participated in the Non-Cooperation Movement and was connected with nationalist political activity in the district.

He organised a group of young revolutionaries who believed that a coordinated uprising could demonstrate that colonial authority could be challenged.

The group acted under the name Indian Republican Army, Chittagong Branch.

The name was inspired by the Irish Republican Army. However, the Chittagong organisation was an Indian revolutionary group pursuing independence from British colonial rule in India.

Important associates of Surya Sen included:

  • Ganesh Ghosh
  • Ananta Singh
  • Lokenath Bal
  • Ambika Chakrabarty

Indian Republican Army, Chittagong Branch: Surya Sen's revolutionary organisation in Bengal.
Hindustan Republican Association: The earlier organisation established in northern India in 1924.
Hindustan Socialist Republican Association: The organisation reorganised in Delhi in 1928.

These similar names do not identify the same organisation.

The Chittagong Armoury Raid: 18 April 1930

The Chittagong Armoury Raid occurred on the night of 18 April 1930.

Under Surya Sen's overall leadership, revolutionary groups seized important colonial armoury facilities in Chittagong and disrupted communications. They intended to challenge British authority and demonstrate the possibility of organised resistance.

The revolutionaries raised the national flag and proclaimed a provisional revolutionary government. This proclamation was a symbolic rejection of British rule rather than the establishment of a lasting government controlling the region.

The group was unable to maintain control of Chittagong. British forces soon moved against the revolutionaries.

The Jalalabad Hills Encounter: 22 April 1930

After the raid, the revolutionaries withdrew towards the surrounding hills.

On 22 April 1930, they fought British forces at the Jalalabad Hills near Chittagong.

Several revolutionaries were killed, and the British government intensified its efforts to capture the remaining participants. Surya Sen and other surviving members continued underground resistance for some time.

The Chittagong action therefore did not result in permanent revolutionary control of the town. Its immediate consequence was a major confrontation followed by extensive colonial repression.

Women Associated with the Chittagong Movement

Women also became active participants in the later revolutionary activities associated with the Chittagong organisation.

Kalpana Dutt

Kalpana Dutt, also written Kalpana Datta, joined Surya Sen's revolutionary circle after the original armoury raid, in 1931.

She participated in subsequent revolutionary activities and was later arrested and sentenced to transportation for life in a related Chittagong conspiracy prosecution.

Her association with the Chittagong movement should not be taken to mean that she was physically present during the original raid of 18 April 1930.

Pritilata Waddedar

Pritilata Waddedar was another revolutionary associated with Surya Sen's movement. In 1932, she led an attack on the Pahartali European Club near Chittagong and died during the aftermath of that action.

Her activities demonstrated that women participated in revolutionary action and were not confined to supporting roles.

Arrest and Execution of Surya Sen

Surya Sen continued revolutionary activity after the 1930 raid while avoiding arrest.

He was eventually captured on 16 February 1933.

Following prosecution by the colonial government, Surya Sen was executed at Chittagong on 12 January 1934.

The British response to the Chittagong movement included extensive searches, arrests, trials, severe prison sentences and collective punitive measures against communities suspected of supporting revolutionaries.

Prelims focus

  • Surya Sen, popularly known as Masterda, led the Chittagong revolutionary group.
  • The organisation acted as the Indian Republican Army, Chittagong Branch.
  • The Chittagong Armoury Raid took place on 18 April 1930.
  • The Jalalabad Hills encounter occurred on 22 April 1930.
  • Surya Sen was captured on 16 February 1933 and executed on 12 January 1934.
  • Kalpana Dutt and Pritilata Waddedar were associated with the subsequent Chittagong revolutionary movement.
  • Trap: The Indian Republican Army at Chittagong was distinct from the HRA and HSRA. Kalpana Dutt joined the movement after the original raid.

[Sources: Indira Gandhi National Open University, History of India VIII (c. 1857–1950), Unit 9, sections 9.9–9.10, printed pp. 128–130, consulted 21 November 2026; Government of Tamil Nadu, SCERT, Higher Secondary Second Year History, Vol. 1, 2019, Unit 5, Period of Radicalism in Anti-imperialist Struggles, printed pp. 67–68; Banglapedia, entry Kalpana Datta, consulted 21 November 2026.]

body:
Distinguishing the Principal Revolutionary Organisations

The revolutionary organisations of the Indian national movement operated in different regions and periods. Some developed from earlier secret societies, while others emerged through the reorganisation of surviving revolutionaries.

Correctly matching an organisation with its leader, location, year and major action is essential for distinguishing these movements.

OrganisationPrincipal centre and leadersMajor event or association
Anushilan Samiti, around 1902Calcutta; Pramathanath Mitra and other early organisersEarly revolutionary organisation in Bengal; later associated networks faced the Alipore prosecutions
Dhaka Anushilan Samiti, 1906Dhaka; Pulin Behari DasExpansion of organised revolutionary activity in eastern Bengal
Jugantar, 1906Bengal; Barindra Kumar Ghosh and associatesRevolutionary newspaper and associated underground group
HRA, 1924Northern India; Sachindranath Sanyal, Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee and Ram Prasad BismilKakori train action, 9 August 1925
HSRA, 1928Delhi, Punjab and northern India; Bhagat Singh, Chandrashekhar Azad and associatesSaunders killing, 1928; Central Legislative Assembly bombing, 1929
Indian Republican Army, Chittagong Branch, 1930Chittagong; Surya SenChittagong Armoury Raid, 18 April 1930

Important Historical Relationships

HRA and HSRA

The HSRA developed through the reorganisation of the HRA. The HRA was established in 1924, while the HSRA emerged in September 1928. The Kakori action therefore belonged to the earlier organisation.

Anushilan Samiti and Jugantar

The 2 names were associated with overlapping revolutionary networks in Bengal, but they did not identify a single uniform organisation. Anushilan began as an organised revolutionary society, whereas Jugantar was the name of a revolutionary newspaper launched in 1906 and the circle associated with it.

HSRA and the Chittagong Indian Republican Army

The HSRA was associated with Bhagat Singh and Chandrashekhar Azad, while the Chittagong Indian Republican Army was associated with Surya Sen. Their similar use of the word Republican does not establish that they were the same organisation.

Match the Incident with Its Correct Historical Outcome

EventYearPrincipal colonial response or result
Muzaffarpur incident1908Khudiram Bose arrested and executed; investigation contributed to the Alipore prosecutions
Alipore Bomb Case1908–1909Aurobindo Ghosh acquitted; several other revolutionaries convicted
Kakori train action1925Kakori Conspiracy Case; 4 revolutionaries executed in December 1927
Saunders killing1928Investigation and prosecution connected with the Lahore Conspiracy Case
Central Legislative Assembly bombing1929Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt arrested and tried
Chittagong Armoury Raid1930British military and police response; Surya Sen captured in 1933 and executed in 1934

Understanding the Chronological Sequence

The broad development began with secret revolutionary societies in Bengal during the early 1900s. The movement subsequently developed stronger organisational links in northern India, particularly after 1922.

The founding of the HRA in 1924 was followed by the Kakori action in 1925 and the execution of important revolutionaries in 1927. The reorganisation of surviving revolutionaries produced the HSRA in 1928.

Bhagat Singh and his associates carried out major revolutionary actions in 1928 and 1929. Meanwhile, Surya Sen's Chittagong group undertook a coordinated uprising in 1930.

These events overlapped with other forms of nationalist protest. Their chronology should therefore be understood as the development of several revolutionary groups, not as a sequence in which every new organisation replaced all earlier organisations.

Common Distinctions in Objective Questions

  • Organisation versus incident: Kakori was an action undertaken by members of the HRA, not the name of a revolutionary organisation.
  • Leader versus participant: Surya Sen led the Chittagong movement; Ganesh Ghosh and Ananta Singh were among his important associates.
  • Target versus person killed: James A. Scott was the intended target of the December 1928 retaliation, but J. P. Saunders was killed.
  • Assembly participants versus those executed: Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt participated in the Assembly bombing; Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were executed in 1931.
  • Death in an encounter versus execution: Chandrashekhar Azad died during a police encounter on 27 February 1931; Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were executed on 23 March 1931.
  • Place in British India versus present location: Chittagong was in eastern Bengal during the colonial period and is now in Bangladesh.

Prelims focus

  • 1902: Early development of Anushilan Samiti in Calcutta.
  • 1906: Dhaka Anushilan Samiti under Pulin Behari Das; emergence of the Jugantar weekly.
  • 1924–1925: Formation of the HRA followed by the Kakori action.
  • 1928–1929: Formation of the HSRA, Saunders killing and Assembly bombing.
  • 1930–1934: Chittagong raid, Jalalabad encounter, arrest and execution of Surya Sen.
  • Trap: HRA, HSRA and the Indian Republican Army of Chittagong were distinct organisational identities, despite similarities in their names and their common opposition to British colonial rule.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-III, Class 8, chapter The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 113–120; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World-II, Class 10, chapter Nationalism in India, printed p. 65; Government of Tamil Nadu, SCERT, Higher Secondary Second Year History, Vol. 1, 2019, Unit 2, printed pp. 22–24, and Unit 5, printed pp. 66–68; Indira Gandhi National Open University, History of India VIII (c. 1857–1950), Unit 9, sections 9.6–9.10, printed pp. 124–130, consulted 21 November 2026.]
